event_overview.title: About Iran War
event_overview.subject: Iran War
event_overview.summary: The Iran War is the 2026 armed conflict involving the United States, Iran and Israel, centered on attacks, counterattacks and threats affecting Iran, neighboring states and maritime traffic in and around the Persian Gulf and Strait of Hormuz. U.S. officials said combat operations began on February 28, 2026, citing self-defense, protection of regional forces and allies, and freedom of maritime commerce; the United Nations has called for de-escalation, protection of civilians and compliance with international law.

facts.label: Start and parties
facts.value: The conflict’s current phase began on February 28, 2026. The United States notified the UN that it had commenced combat operations against Iran in cooperation with Israel; the UN Secretary-General also described subsequent Iranian attacks affecting Bahrain, Iraq, Jordan, Kuwait, Qatar, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates.

facts.label: Geographic focus
facts.value: The Strait of Hormuz—between Iran and Oman, linking the Persian Gulf with the Gulf of Oman and Arabian Sea—is a central theater because its security directly affects regional shipping and energy exports.

facts.label: Maritime and energy stakes
facts.value: Disruption to shipping through Hormuz has been a major international consequence: EIA reported that military action and the resulting de facto closure sharply reduced oil flows and contributed to large price increases in early 2026.

facts.label: Diplomatic and legal framework
facts.value: The UN has urged an immediate cessation of hostilities and stated that all parties must uphold the UN Charter, protect civilians under international humanitarian law and preserve nuclear safety. In the United States, the War Powers Resolution requires presidential consultation with Congress where possible and a written report within 48 hours when U.S. forces are introduced into hostilities without a declaration of wa

facts.label: Broader policy context
facts.value: The conflict occurs alongside longstanding international concern over Iran’s nuclear programme. UN Security Council Resolution 2231, adopted in 2015 to endorse the JCPOA, remains part of that background; the UN says earlier Iran-related Security Council measures were re-applied on September 27, 2025.

event_overview.scope_note: The selected Muninn timeline focuses on late-July 2026 escalation, congressional war-powers action, Houthi-linked regional attacks, oil-market effects and ceasefire diplomacy; it does not attempt to document the conflict’s full military, humanitarian, diplomatic or legal history.

explore_lenses.title: A coastal-state role, not just mediation
explore_lenses.summary: Oman’s role stems from its territorial waters in the Strait of Hormuz and its stated effort to negotiate a lawful, durable navigation arrangement with Iran and shipping users.

claims.text: Oman and Iran said on June 23 that, as the Strait’s two coastal states, they would continue foreign-ministry working-group talks on navigation administration, services and costs, while pledging safe passage consistent with international law.
Oman’s foreign minister has argued that Muscat has a special responsibility to work both with Iran and the wider community of Strait users to achieve free navigation.
Oman says its cooperation is neutral and must comply with the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea; its position is therefore broader than a bilateral Iran-Oman shipping arrangement.

explore_lenses.summary: The current dispute follows an earlier U.S.-Iran framework that reopened the Strait and left longer-term issues for negotiation, but later hostilities disrupted that process.

claims.text: The UN said on June 15 that the United States and Iran had agreed to an immediate, permanent ceasefire, reopening of the Strait, and a framework for further negotiations.

Oman and Iran subsequently said their discussions on the Strait were being conducted under the provisions of the Islamabad memorandum of understanding and would continue through a joint working group.

By July 13, the UN reported renewed Iranian attacks on ships, U.S. attacks on Iran, and Iranian attacks on neighboring-country targets; the Secretary-General called for an urgent return to negotiations and restoration of full freedom of navigation.
Iran’s UN representative has argued that durable maritime safety requires an end to what Tehran calls U.S. aggression and respect for the sovereignty and sovereign rights of coastal states.

sections.heading: Oman and Iran Navigation Talks
sections.body: Oman and Iran said on June 23 that, as the Strait’s two coastal states, they would continue foreign-ministry working-group talks on navigation administration, services and costs while pledging safe passage consistent with international law. They later agreed to continue technical and political discussions intended to produce the understandings needed for safe and free navigation. Oman has described its role as neutral cooperation governed by the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea and involving the broader community of Strait users, rather than a solely bilateral arrangement.

sections.heading: Ceasefire Framework Faces Renewed Fighting
sections.body: The United Nations said on June 15 that Washington and Tehran had agreed to an immediate, permanent ceasefire, the reopening of the Strait and a framework for further negotiations. But by July 13, the UN reported renewed Iranian attacks on ships, U.S. attacks on Iran and Iranian attacks on targets in neighboring countries. The Secretary-General called for an urgent return to negotiations and restoration of full freedom of navigation, warning that a return to full-scale hostilities would have catastrophic regional and global economic consequences.

event_overview.title: About Gaza Peace Deal
event_overview.subject: Gaza Peace Deal
event_overview.summary: The Gaza Peace Deal refers to the U.S.-backed, internationally supported framework to end the Israel-Hamas war in Gaza through a ceasefire, hostage and detainee releases, Hamas’s disarmament and Gaza’s demilitarization, Israeli withdrawals tied to agreed milestones, humanitarian access, and postwar governance and reconstruction. It builds on earlier Egypt-, Qatar-, and U.S.-mediated ceasefire efforts, but its implementation depends on compliance and verification by multiple parties rather than on a single self-executing agreement.

facts.label: Framework and international status
facts.value: President Trump’s Comprehensive Plan is a 20-point roadmap; the United Nations Security Council endorsed the plan in Resolution 2803 (2025) and welcomed a Board of Peace to support its implementation.

facts.label: Core proposed exchange and military step
facts.value: The framework envisages an end to military operations and a staged Israeli withdrawal, alongside the return of hostages and the release of specified Palestinian detainees; further withdrawal is linked to agreed demilitarization standards, milestones, and timeframes.

facts.label: Disarmament and transitional governance
facts.value: A subsequent 15-point implementation roadmap, presented by Egypt, Qatar, Türkiye, the United States, and the High Representative for Gaza, calls for Hamas to end military, policing, and administrative activity and for the National Committee for the Administration of Gaza (NCAG) to serve as the transitional civilian authority.

facts.label: Institutions and outside roles
facts.value: The plan’s implementation architecture includes the Board of Peace, an Office of the High Representative for Gaza, the NCAG, and an International Stabilization Force intended to support security, demilitarization, aid delivery, and reconstruction. Egypt, Qatar, Türkiye, and the United States are identified as guarantors in the UN implementation report.

facts.label: Legal and humanitarian context
facts.value: The International Committee of the Red Cross considers Gaza occupied territory under its effective-control assessment and states that international humanitarian law continues to govern protections for civilians and duties relevant to the territory’s administration and supply.

event_overview.scope_note: The selected Muninn timeline follows reported late-July to mid-August 2026 developments concerning the deal’s implementation, Israeli-Hamas military and political responses, and one related Lebanon escalation; it is not a complete chronology of the Gaza war, all negotiations, humanitarian conditions, or the wider regional conflict.

story_report.summary: A federal judge has halted the Trump administration’s plan to abandon the previously selected Greenbelt, Maryland, site for a new FBI headquarters and instead move the bureau into Washington’s Ronald Reagan Building. The Aug. 17 order vacated the FBI’s and General Services Administration’s 2025 Reagan Building decisions, including a plan to reprogram $555 million for relocation, renovation, build-out and furnishings. A permanent injunction bars agencies from spending or taking further action to support the proposed move.

sections.heading: Court Rejects Reagan Building Plan
sections.body: The court concluded that the Reagan Building decisions were not in accordance with law. It rejected the administration’s position that subsequent congressional measures had ratified the change or implicitly repealed earlier requirements governing the headquarters site selection. Congress had directed GSA in 2022 to choose among Greenbelt and Landover, Maryland, and Springfield, Virginia; GSA announced Greenbelt as the selected location in November 2023.

sections.heading: Greenbelt Selection and FBI Needs
sections.body: GSA said its 2023 selection of Greenbelt reflected the lowest projected site-preparation cost among the three specified sites, rail access, greater schedule certainty, and sustainability and equity considerations. The court also found that the aging J. Edgar Hoover Building could not meet the FBI’s staffing and security needs, while personnel spread across multiple locations in the National Capital Region created operational difficulties. The FBI said the Reagan Building proposal was intended to make government more cost-effective, while Maryland Attorney General Anthony Brown said the ruling protects funds set aside for Greenbelt.

sections.heading: FBI Headquarters Case Next Steps
sections.body: The parties must submit a joint status report within 14 days of the Aug. 17 order, proposing next steps and stating whether the case can be closed. The court said the injunction could be reconsidered if Congress enacts legislation changing or rescinding the site-selection provisions. Separately, the 2026 appropriations law prevents further obligation of specified reprogrammed funds until the FBI provides a completed architectural and engineering plan; the court said none had been submitted when it ruled.

event_overview.summary: The Gaza Peace Deal refers to the U.S.-backed, internationally supported framework to end the Israel-Hamas war in Gaza through a ceasefire, hostage and detainee releases, Hamas’s disarmament and Gaza’s demilitarization, Israeli withdrawals tied to agreed milestones, humanitarian access, and postwar governance and reconstruction. It builds on earlier Egypt-, Qatar-, and U.S.-mediated ceasefire efforts, but its implementation depends on compliance and verification by multiple parties rather than on a single self-executing agreement.

facts.label: Framework and international status
facts.value: President Trump’s Comprehensive Plan is a 20-point roadmap; the United Nations Security Council endorsed the plan in Resolution 2803 (2025) and welcomed a Board of Peace to support its implementation.

facts.label: Core proposed exchange and military step
facts.value: The framework envisages an end to military operations and a staged Israeli withdrawal, alongside the return of hostages and the release of specified Palestinian detainees; further withdrawal is linked to agreed demilitarization standards, milestones, and timeframes.

facts.label: Disarmament and transitional governance
facts.value: A subsequent 15-point implementation roadmap, presented by Egypt, Qatar, Türkiye, the United States, and the High Representative for Gaza, calls for Hamas to end military, policing, and administrative activity and for the National Committee for the Administration of Gaza (NCAG) to serve as the transitional civilian authority.

facts.label: Institutions and outside roles
facts.value: The plan’s implementation architecture includes the Board of Peace, an Office of the High Representative for Gaza, the NCAG, and an International Stabilization Force intended to support security, demilitarization, aid delivery, and reconstruction. Egypt, Qatar, Türkiye, and the United States are identified as guarantors in the UN implementation report.

facts.label: Legal and humanitarian context
facts.value: The International Committee of the Red Cross considers Gaza occupied territory under its effective-control assessment and states that international humanitarian law continues to govern protections for civilians and duties relevant to the territory’s administration and supply.

story_report.summary: A murder trial has opened in the 1996 drive-by killing of Tupac Shakur, nearly 30 years after the rapper was shot. Prosecutors allege Duane “Keffe D” Davis ordered a retaliatory attack after his nephew, Orlando Anderson, was beaten at the MGM Grand; they do not contend Davis fired the shots. Davis, the first person charged in the long-running cold case, has pleaded not guilty and could face life in prison without parole if convicted.

sections.heading: Prosecutors Detail Davis’s Alleged Role
sections.body: Prosecutors played material from Davis’s 2008 interview and plan to rely on his 2019 co-authored memoir. They say those accounts describe Davis handing a gun to men seated in the back of a Cadillac before the shooting. Authorities have said neither the white Cadillac nor the weapon was recovered, while the three other men allegedly in the vehicle have died.

sections.heading: Defense Challenges Evidence Against Davis
sections.body: Defense lawyer Michael Sanft called the prosecution’s account “fiction,” arguing that the investigation was biased, sloppy and incomplete and that the passage of time has weakened recollections. Sanft had also argued that detectives promised Davis his 2008 interview would not be used against him, but Judge Carli Kierny ruled it admissible. Prosecutors say Davis’s later memoir and public comments weaken that argument; the defense says the memoir was fictionalized for profit.

sections.heading: Jury Faces Month-Long Davis Trial
sections.body: The Associated Press reported that prosecutors planned to call about 35 to 45 witnesses and expected the trial to last roughly a month. The prosecution’s theory does not require it to establish that Davis fired the fatal shots, and the shooter’s identity could remain unresolved even if jurors conclude Davis organized or assisted the attack.

unresolved.text: Jurors must determine what weight to give Davis’s interview statements and memoir, including whether they are accurate admissions, embellishment or both, and whether the remaining evidence proves his alleged role beyond a reasonable doubt.

event_overview.title: About Congo Ebola Outbreak
event_overview.subject: Congo Ebola Outbreak
event_overview.summary: This is the 2026 Ebola disease outbreak caused by Bundibugyo virus in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), with epidemiologically linked cases reported in neighboring Uganda. The outbreak was declared in May 2026 and has expanded from its initial focus in northeastern DRC amid insecurity, population movement, and constraints on surveillance, isolation, and care.

facts.label: Start and official declaration
facts.value: DRC health authorities declared the country’s 17th recorded Ebola outbreak on May 15, 2026, after the Institut National de Recherche Biomédicale confirmed Bundibugyo virus disease in samples associated with illness clusters in Ituri Province.

facts.label: Virus involved
facts.value: The event involves Bundibugyo virus disease, rather than the Zaire ebolavirus responsible for DRC’s 2018–2020 outbreak. WHO states that no approved vaccine or specific treatment existed for this virus as the 2026 outbreak began, although candidate countermeasures were being studied.

facts.label: Geographic scope
facts.value: Transmission began in Ituri Province, including Mongbwalu, Rwampara and Bunia health zones, and later spread to other DRC provinces. Uganda’s cases were linked to transmission originating in DRC, making this a cross-border regional outbreak rather than an outbreak confined to one locality.

facts.label: International health status

event_overview.title: About Gaza Peace Deal
event_overview.subject: Gaza Peace Deal
event_overview.summary: The Gaza Peace Deal refers to the U.S.-backed, internationally supported framework to end the Israel-Hamas war in Gaza through a ceasefire, hostage and detainee releases, Hamas’s disarmament and Gaza’s demilitarization, Israeli withdrawals tied to agreed milestones, humanitarian access, and postwar governance and reconstruction. It builds on earlier Egypt-, Qatar-, and U.S.-mediated ceasefire efforts, but its implementation depends on compliance and verification by multiple parties rather than on a single self-executing agreement.

facts.label: Framework and international status
facts.value: President Trump’s Comprehensive Plan is a 20-point roadmap; the United Nations Security Council endorsed the plan in Resolution 2803 (2025) and welcomed a Board of Peace to support its implementation.

facts.label: Core proposed exchange and military step
facts.value: The framework envisages an end to military operations and a staged Israeli withdrawal, alongside the return of hostages and the release of specified Palestinian detainees; further withdrawal is linked to agreed demilitarization standards, milestones, and timeframes.

facts.label: Disarmament and transitional governance
facts.value: A subsequent 15-point implementation roadmap, presented by Egypt, Qatar, Türkiye, the United States, and the High Representative for Gaza, calls for Hamas to end military, policing, and administrative activity and for the National Committee for the Administration of Gaza (NCAG) to serve as the transitional civilian authority.

facts.label: Institutions and outside roles
facts.value: The plan’s implementation architecture includes the Board of Peace, an Office of the High Representative for Gaza, the NCAG, and an International Stabilization Force intended to support security, demilitarization, aid delivery, and reconstruction. Egypt, Qatar, Türkiye, and the United States are identified as guarantors in the UN implementation report.

facts.label: Legal and humanitarian context
facts.value: The International Committee of the Red Cross considers Gaza occupied territory under its effective-control assessment and states that international humanitarian law continues to govern protections for civilians and duties relevant to the territory’s administration and supply.

highlights.title: Trump Directs Military to Reduce Joint Exercises with South Korea
highlights.summary: President Trump has ordered the Pentagon to substantially reduce joint military exercises with South Korea, citing the country's refusal to assist in denuclearizing Iran and his positive relationship with North Korea's leader, Kim Jong-un. The decision comes just before the start of the Ulchi Freedom Shield exercises, which are designed to deter North Korean aggression. Military officials have expressed concerns that scaling back these drills may embolden North Korea amid its increasing military capabilities.
key_facts: Trump ordered a reduction in joint military exercises with South Korea.
The decision was influenced by South Korea's stance on Iran and Trump's relationship with Kim Jong-un.
Concerns have been raised about the implications of reduced military readiness against North Korea.

event_overview.title: About US-South Korea Relations
event_overview.subject: US-South Korea Relations
event_overview.summary: The developments concern a reported direction to reduce U.S.-Republic of Korea combined military training, a recurring element of the two countries’ security alliance. Any such change would affect exercises used to rehearse combined command, interoperability and responses to contingencies on the Korean Peninsula.

facts.label: Alliance basis
facts.value: The U.S.-ROK security relationship is grounded in the Mutual Defense Treaty signed on October 1, 1953; U.S. Forces Korea describes recent combined exercises as operating in the treaty’s spirit.

facts.label: Main exercise framework
facts.value: Freedom Shield and Ulchi Freedom Shield are annual combined exercises involving the Republic of Korea and the United States; Ulchi Freedom Shield is described by USFK as combined, joint, all-domain and interagency training.

facts.label: Participants and command structure
facts.value: USFK identifies the Combined Forces Command, U.S. Forces Korea, United Nations Command, the ROK Joint Chiefs of Staff and ROK government agencies as participants in Ulchi Freedom Shield. Freedom Shield is conducted under the Combined Forces Command.

facts.label: Format and stated purpose
facts.value: The exercises combine live, virtual, constructive and field-based training. USFK says their stated purposes include strengthening combined readiness, interoperability and the alliance’s ability to respond to security threats; it characterizes Freedom Shield as defensive in nature.

facts.label: Recent baseline
facts.value: Freedom Shield 26 ran from March 9 to March 19, 2026, and included Warrior Shield, field training across the Korean Peninsula involving ground, maritime, air and Marine forces.

event_overview.scope_note: The selected Muninn timeline covers the August 17-18, 2026 policy developments concerning reductions in joint exercises, not the full history of the U.S.-ROK alliance, all military training, or subsequent implementation details.
